title: Probability: Outcomes, Relative Frequency and Probability
seo_title: Grade 7 Probability Worksheets with Answers (CAPS Maths)
standard_text: Perform simple experiments where the possible outcomes are equally likely and list the possible outcomes based on the conditions of the activity; determine probabilities for each possible outcome; determine the relative frequency of the actual outcomes for a series of trials; compare relative frequency with probability and explain possible differences.
meta_desc: Free CAPS Grade 7 probability worksheets: the probability scale, single events, sample spaces and relative frequency. 100 questions with memos.
body_html:
How to think about it

  • Probability = number of favourable outcomes ÷ number of possible outcomes.
  • Probabilities go from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
  • P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
  • Relative frequency = number of times an outcome happened ÷ number of trials. With more trials it gets closer to the probability.

Examples

Example

A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green beads

10 beads

not red: 7

Answer: P(not red) = 7/10

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
More than 1A probability is at most 1.
Counting twiceList the outcomes carefully.
Relative frequency = probabilityIt comes from an experiment and changes.

items.q: A fair dice is rolled 300 times. How many times would you expect to get a 6?
items.e: Expected number = probability × number of trials = 16 × 300 = 50.

items.q: Three coins are flipped. What is the probability of getting three heads?
items.e: There are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes and only HHH works: 18.

items.q: Two coins are flipped. What is the probability of getting one head and one tail?
items.e: Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. Two of the four work (HT and TH): 12.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability of a total of 3?
items.e: There are 36 outcomes. A total of 3 comes from (1, 2), (2, 1): 2 ways, so P = 236 = 118.

items.q: A fair dice is rolled 120 times. How many times would you expect to get an even number?
items.e: Expected number = probability × number of trials = 12 × 120 = 60.

items.q: A coin is flipped and a fair dice is rolled. How many possible outcomes are there?
items.e: 2 outcomes for the coin × 6 for the dice = 12.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability of a total of 5?
items.e: There are 36 outcomes. A total of 5 comes from (1, 4), (2, 3), (3, 2), (4, 1): 4 ways, so P = 436 = 19.

items.q: Two fair dice are rolled and the scores are added. What is the probability of a total of 10?
items.e: There are 36 outcomes. A total of 10 comes from (4, 6), (5, 5), (6, 4): 3 ways, so P = 336 = 112.

items.q: You toss a coin and spin a spinner with 2 equal sections, red and blue. Which list shows all the outcomes? (H = heads, T = tails, R = red, B = blue)
items.e: Pair each coin face with each colour: 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes, HR, HB, TR, TB. H, T, R, B lists single results, not pairs. HT is not possible: there is only one coin.

items.q: You toss two coins. Which list shows the whole sample space?
items.e: The first coin can be H or T, and so can the second: 2 × 2 = 4 outcomes, HH, HT, TH, TT. HT and TH are different: heads on the first coin is not the same as heads on the second.

items.q: How many outcomes does the tree diagram show?
items.e: Each of the 2 coin branches splits into 3 colours: 2 × 3 = 6 outcomes. 5 comes from adding 2 + 3.

items.q: Which outcome is NOT in the sample space?
items.e: The spinner only has red, blue and yellow, so H, green can’t happen. The other three are all at the end of a branch.

items.q: How many branches come out of H?
items.e: After heads, the spinner can land on 1, 2, 3 or 4, so 4 branches come out of H. 8 is the number of outcomes in the whole tree.

items.q: How many outcomes in the table show tails?
items.e: The tails row has T1, T2, T3, T4, T5 and T6: 6 outcomes. 12 is the whole table.

items.q: How many outcomes show heads and an odd number?
items.e: Heads and odd: H1, H3 and H5, so 3 outcomes. 6 counts the odd numbers with tails too.

items.q: How many outcomes show a 6?
items.e: A 6 can come with heads or with tails: H6 and T6, so 2 outcomes. 1 forgets that the coin can land either way.

items.q: You toss a coin and roll a number cube with the numbers 1 to 6. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: Each coin face goes with each of the 6 numbers: 2 × 6 = 12. 8 comes from adding 2 + 6.

items.q: You spin spinner A and spinner B. How many outcomes are there?
items.e: Each colour goes with each of the 4 numbers: 2 × 4 = 8. 6 comes from adding 2 + 4.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of HH, as a decimal?
items.e: HH came up 12 times in 50 tosses: 1250 = 24100 = 0,24. 0,25 is the theoretical probability. 0,12 uses the count as the decimal.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of one head and one tail, as a decimal?
items.e: One head and one tail is HT or TH: 13 + 14 = 27 times. 2750 = 54100 = 0,54. 0,5 is the theoretical probability.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of TT, as a percent?
items.e: TT came up 11 times in 50: 1150 = 22100 = 22%. 11% uses the count as the percent. 78% is NOT TT.

items.q: Which outcome has an experimental probability of 0,28?
items.e: 0,28 = 28100 = 1450. TH came up 14 times, so the answer is TH.

items.q: Dumisani tosses a coin and rolls a number cube 60 times. He gets heads and a 6 four times. What is the experimental probability of heads and a 6?
items.e: Experimental probability = times it happened ÷ number of trials = 460. 112 is the theoretical probability. 456 compares with the other trials, not with all 60.

items.q: Chloe rolls two number cubes 90 times. The sum is 7 on 18 rolls. What is the experimental probability of a sum of 7?
items.e: 1890 = 15. 16 is the theoretical probability, not what happened. 1872 divides by the rolls that were not 7.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of blue, 2 as a percent?
items.e: Blue, 2 came up 14 times in 40 spins: 1440 = 35100 = 35%. 14% uses the count as the percent. 25% is the theory.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of blue with either number, as a decimal?
items.e: Blue, 1 and blue, 2: 6 + 14 = 20 times. 2040 = 0,5. 0,35 uses only blue, 2, and 0,15 only blue, 1.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of a 1 with either colour, as a decimal?
items.e: Red, 1 and blue, 1: 11 + 6 = 17 times. 1740 = 17 ÷ 40 = 0,425. 0,275 uses only red, 1. 0,5 is the theory.

items.q: What is the experimental probability of H, yellow as a percent?
items.e: H, yellow came up 12 times in 60: 1260 = 15 = 20%. About 17% is the theory (16). 12% uses the count as the percent.

items.q: You toss a coin and roll a number cube 120 times. About how many times would you expect heads and a 6?
items.e: Heads and 6 is 112. 112 of 120 = 120 ÷ 12 = about 10. About 15 comes from 120 ÷ 8 (adding 2 + 6 outcomes). About 20 uses 16 only.

items.q: You toss two coins 200 times. About how many times would you expect two heads?
items.e: P(HH) = 14. 14 of 200 = about 50. About 67 uses 13, which forgets that HT and TH are different.

items.q: You roll two number cubes 360 times. About how many times would you expect a sum of 7?
items.e: P(sum of 7) = 636 = 16. 360 ÷ 6 = about 60. About 33 treats the 11 sums as equally likely. About 10 uses only one of the 6 ways to make 7.

items.q: You spin both spinners 80 times. About how many times would you expect each outcome?
items.e: There are 8 equally likely outcomes, so each has probability 18. 80 ÷ 8 = about 10. About 13 comes from 80 ÷ 6 (adding 2 + 4 outcomes).

items.q: The theoretical probability of two heads is 0,25. Group A tosses two coins 20 times and gets HH 8 times. Group B tosses them 400 times and gets HH 96 times. Whose experimental probability is closer to 0,25?
items.e: Group A: 820 = 0,4. Group B: 96400 = 0,24. 0,24 is much closer to 0,25, so Group B’s is closer.

items.q: Why are the results of 400 trials usually closer to the theory than the results of 20 trials?
c: More trials usually get closer to the theory
The coins wear out after 20 tosses
Big experiments always match the theory exactly
items.e: With only a few trials, luck changes the results a lot. More trials usually get closer to the theoretical probability, but not exactly.

items.q: Daniel tosses two coins 10 times and gets HH 4 times. He says the coins must be unfair because 0,4 is not 0,25. Is he right?
c: No, 10 trials are too few to tell
No, HH can never come up 4 times
Yes, HH should come up exactly 2,5 times
items.e: With only 10 trials, results can be far from the theory just by chance. 10 trials are too few to tell. He should do many more trials.

items.q: Two coins are tossed 1 000 times and HH comes up 381 times. What do the results suggest?
c: 1 000 trials are too few to tell
HH will now come up less often
The coins are probably not fair
items.e: Theory: 14 of 1 000 = 250. 381 is far from 250 after a lot of trials, so the coins are probably not fair.

items.q: The experimental probability of an outcome is 0,3 and the theoretical probability is 0,25. What is the difference?
items.e: 0,30 − 0,25 = 0,05. 0,55 adds them instead of subtracting.

items.q: The theoretical probability of heads and an even number is 14. Which experimental result is closest to the theory?
items.e: As decimals: 0,26; 0,4; 0,35 and 0,5. 14 = 0,25, so 26 out of 100 is closest.
